work.title: Homily on the sinful woman (Holy Wednesday)

paragraphs.text: A sermon by John Chrysostom, archbishop, on the prostitute, for Holy Wednesday before Easter [?]. Repentance is good and brings salvation at every season to those who hold fast to it. But especially in these days of fasting, it benefits everyone who runs into its arms. For now our souls have cast off the heavy flesh, like a great burden, and fly readily to the Creator and Master. They rebuke themselves for their own sins and ask forgiveness for their transgressions from the Judge who loves mankind. It is therefore timely for us to introduce a teacher of repentance, that prostitute who embraced the pure feet of Christ the Master. With drops of tears she erased the record of her wicked life; he cleansed her in mercy and washed her in compassion. Let us therefore turn to the Gospel account, so that we may see Christ’s love for mankind and marvel at the woman’s approach, and learn from her that we sinners too must run to the Redeemer in this way and receive from him freedom from punishment for our sins. A certain Pharisee asked the Lord to eat with him, and he entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined at the table. Do you see how awe-inspiring his condescension is? Do you see the mystery of God’s providence? Do you see the abundance of his love for mankind? He who gives food

to all flesh was invited to dinner by his own servant and came to him without hesitation, so that through this invitation he might show the loftiness of his condescension. He came as a man into the Pharisee’s dwelling, though he fills every place, so that he might show both God’s providence and his love for mankind. And behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner learned that he was reclining at the table in the Pharisee’s house. She brought a glass jar of fragrant ointment and stood behind him at his feet, weeping, and began to wet his feet with her tears. She wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet, and anointed them with perfume, saying nothing aloud to him. For she feared that some unclean word might come from her sinful lips and stir the Judge to anger against her. But she prayed in silence, making her confession with her heart alone, and offered her supplication to the Master, who alone knows what is in the heart. In her mind she cried out to him as to one who loves mankind: “I have dared to approach you, Lord.” for the sake of your mother, the Virgin, as you alone know, Creator and God. Therefore, for the sake of your virgin mother, who knew no marriage, have mercy on me, a prostitute. Grant me forgiveness for my sins. For the sake of her virginity, forgive my prostitution. Have mercy on me,

Lover of humanity, as I weep—you who rightly hated me when I laughed wickedly. Have mercy on me as I groan with all my soul—you who rightly turned away from me as I adorned my body to bring ruin and temptation to many. Have mercy on the braids that you yourself made to adorn my head, but which I arranged to bring ruin upon my soul. Accept this myrrh as heavenly myrrh, and cover the filth of my life. Accept this myrrh, and secretly grant me spiritual myrrh. Source of good things, wash me, who have defiled myself. Almighty physician, heal me, who have received many wounds from the devil. Scrape away the sinful stains of my soul, as you scraped away the bodily affliction of the faithful leper. Dry up the fountain of my lawless deeds, as you dried up the rivers of the bleeding woman by the hem of your garment. Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David, as you had mercy on that Canaanite woman, who was not of that people but was faithful. As the prostitute thus faithfully and secretly, in her soul's workshop, prayed with tears, everyone marveled at Jesus' patience, seeing him meekly endure the prostitute's kisses and the touch of her sinful hands. But the Pharisee who had invited him to dinner was secretly forging blasphemous thoughts against him in the workshop of his soul, and maligning the Savior's love for humanity, as though he were ignorant.

He said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would know what kind of woman is touching him, that she is a sinner.” Truly, the Pharisee's understanding was inhuman and blind. But what did the good benefactor say to him? “Simon, Simon, I have something to say to you. I have heard the words you have not spoken. I have understood the thoughts of your soul. I know what you thought against me in your mind. Therefore, although you have said nothing, I answer openly, so that from my answer you may know the power of my divinity, so that from my words you may understand that I am the Creator of souls and the knower of hearts. For whether you wish to call me a prophet or the Creator of prophets, whom you see as a man, believe as you wish. Simon, Simon, I have something to say to you. There were two debtors.” Someone had lent money. One man owed five hundred silver coins, and the other fifty. Since neither of them had the means to repay him, he forgave them both. Which of them will love him more? Simon answered, “I suppose the one who was forgiven more.” The Savior said to him, “You have judged correctly. You too owe me many debts from your life, and I forgive you the sins of your life, just as I forgive this woman. When you invited me,

I immediately answered you there, and came under the same roof and shared the same meal—not as someone poor or lacking food, but as one rich in mercy, bringing those who come to me to repentance and forgiving their sins. Why do you speak against my coming down? Why do you malign my love for humanity, with which you yourself have already been filled? Why do you [?] so much about others, about my purity, which, if I show it to you now, will do you no good? Why do you measure my goodness, of which you have received only a little?” And turning toward the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman?” Oh, the height of his great love for humanity! Oh, the boundless abundance of his patience! Though she was a prostitute, he did not call her a prostitute, but a woman. Speaking gently, he concealed the name of the devil’s work and called her by the name common to her nature. “Do you see this woman, whom I saw beforehand with the eyes of my divinity, who came to us uninvited, who first acted shamelessly—a good shamelessness—who at the proper time displayed a shamelessness that brings life, whom you slandered after she came to life? She did not dare, as though she had no face, to stand face to face, but hid behind, her former life becoming a reproach to her. I entered your house, and you gave me no water for my feet. But she wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head. The feet

that the sea did not wet with its waves, she wet with her tears, and she pleads with kisses. When have you ever seen a woman make her own hair into a towel, as she has done for my feet? You gave me no kiss, although, being [?], you invited us to dinner. You should first have come out to kiss me and honor me in every way. But you did not do this. But ever since she entered your house, she has not stopped kissing my feet. See her insatiable love, and soften your slander-loving mind. Look at her and observe her weeping.” So that you too may love her whom you hated without reason. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she anointed my feet with perfume. Therefore I tell you: her many sins are forgiven. To him, our God, be glory and power, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
